planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in lean, sharply drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Aglandau is self-sterile, so plant a compatible cultivar such as Picholine or Leccino nearby to ensure good fruit set.

directions: Aglandau is a heritage cultivar from the hill country of Haute-Provence, prized in French groves for producing oil with a bold, green, artichoke-and-almond character, and it is one of the more cold-hardy French olive cultivars, tolerating brief dips into the low teens Fahrenheit better than many Mediterranean selections once established. It is self-sterile, so a compatible second cultivar such as Picholine or Leccino should be planted nearby to ensure a good fruit set. The tree carries narrow, willowy foliage and bears medium, elongated olives that are typically pressed for oil while still green rather than cured as a table fruit. Expect slow establishment in the first few years in lean, sharply drained, alkaline soil, followed by strong, reliable production once the tree matures.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension - Olive Varieties

common_name: Cailletier Olive (Niçoise Olive, Cold-Tolerant French Dual-Purpose Olive)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, low-fertility soil in full sun; Cailletier is self-fertile so a single tree will bear fruit, though a second cultivar nearby improves yield.

directions: Cailletier is the classic small black olive of Nice, brine-cured to produce the true Niçoise olive used in the region's namesake salad, and it also presses into a delicately flavored, high-quality oil. Unlike many French cultivars it is self-fertile, so a single tree will set fruit reliably, though planting a second cultivar nearby increases yield. The tree grows large with an erect habit and gracefully weeping outer branches, and it is considered one of the more cold-tolerant table-olive selections, handling short freezes into the low teens Fahrenheit once well established. Harvest fruit at the deep purple-black stage for traditional Niçoise-style curing, or leave it slightly longer for oil pressing.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension - Olive Varieties

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Lucques is only partially self-fertile, so plant it with a compatible cultivar such as Manzanilla or Leccino for the best fruit set.

directions: Lucques is the crescent-shaped green table olive of the Languedoc region of southern France, prized for its firm, fine-textured flesh and mild, nutty flavor once cured. It is only partially self-fertile, so planting it alongside a compatible cultivar such as Manzanilla or Leccino improves fruit set. The distinctive curved, pointed olives are harvested green in early fall specifically for brine-curing rather than oil pressing, since the crescent shape and clean flesh are central to the variety's culinary appeal. Provide full sun and well-drained, lean soil, and protect young trees from hard freezes until they are well established.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension - Olive Varieties
